questions.q: What three parts does a strong resume bullet combine, according to this lesson?
options: An action verb, the specific tool used, and a concrete outcome
A job title, a date range, and a company name
A list of every tool you've ever heard of
A soft skill, a certification name, and a GPA
questions.explain: Action verb + tool + outcome forces specificity: what you did, what you did it with, and what changed because of it.

questions.q: Why is "Completed a BI capstone project" a weak resume bullet?
options: It gives a hiring manager nothing specific to evaluate — no tool, no action, no outcome
It's too long for a resume
It uses too many technical terms
It should be written in the first person instead
questions.explain: A vague summary line tells the reader nothing they can act on. A structured bullet lets them imagine you doing the same work for their team.

questions.q: If you don't have a company-wide business metric for an outcome, what does this lesson recommend?
options: Use an honest technical outcome instead, such as what the pipeline replaced or its scope, rather than inventing a number
Invent a plausible-sounding percentage improvement
Leave the outcome out of the bullet entirely
Use a business metric from an unrelated real company
questions.explain: A made-up number becomes a credibility problem the moment an interviewer asks about it. A real technical detail is honest and still specific.

questions.q: Where should this capstone project go on a career-changer's resume?
options: In a dedicated Projects section positioned above older, unrelated work history
Buried as a single bullet inside an unrelated past job
Only in the cover letter, never on the resume itself
At the very bottom of the resume, after education
questions.explain: A dedicated Projects section near the top tells the reader exactly where to find evidence you can do the job, instead of asking them to dig for it.

questions.q: What's the difference between listing "SQL Server, SSIS, SSRS, Power BI" in a Skills section versus grouping them by capability?
options: Grouping by capability (e.g. "ETL development (SSIS)") signals what you can do with a tool; a bare list only signals exposure to it
There is no meaningful difference — both read identically to a hiring manager
Grouping by capability is only useful for very senior candidates
A bare tool list is always preferred because it's easier to scan
questions.explain: Pairing a capability with the tool that backs it up signals more than just having heard of the tool once.
